strengths: Significance: Theorem 4.1 gives a useful conditional Wasserstein error bound with a forward horizon independent of sampling accuracy. Using Langevin correction to improve initialization provides a concrete way to separate forward regularization from initialization accuracy for norm-subgaussian targets.

Originality: The strongest analytical contribution is Theorem 4.2. Its score-confinement argument and explicit clipping construction convert terminal-time L2 error into exponential-moment control, addressing a substantive obstacle in applying inexact Langevin guarantees.

Presentation and reproducibility: The error decomposition into early stopping, score approximation, and initialization is clear, and the extensive appendices make the arguments inspectable. Section 6 appropriately acknowledges that full discretization remains unresolved. The mathematical analysis and synthetic examples raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central interpretation: The claim that convergence requires only the usual integrated L2 training loss is stronger than the results establish. Theorem 4.2 separately requires b(T1), which is not controlled by J_SM. For stationary Gaussian data, a fixed score bias supported on a shrinking time interval ending at T1 makes J_SM vanish while retaining terminal bias and nonzero sampling error; sufficiently small bias also survives the proposed clipping. Moreover, Theorem 4.1 retains the exponential stability factor I_tau, and the additional uniform condition discussed on page 7 does not follow from Lipschitzness of each estimator or small L2 error. An explicit convergence corollary must state these additional requirements.

Coverage of the claimed data class: For point-mass targets allowed by (A2), any globally Lipschitz estimator satisfying (A1) has b(t) asymptotic to d/(2t) near zero. Consequently, J_SM as defined over [0,T1] is infinite. Early stopping the sampler does not change that loss definition. Equation (4.3) can still be useful, but the J_SM-based convergence discussion requires a truncated loss and an explicit treatment of its dependence on tau.

Technical correctness: Equations (3.3) and (3.5) have inconsistent reverse-process coefficients: with the stated forward SDE, the score coefficient should be M g^2/2 and the diffusion magnitude sqrt(M-1) g. The final assertion of Lemma 5.6 is also false as stated. Taking d=1, p a point mass at sqrt(2/3), and t=log(sqrt(2)) satisfies its threshold but gives KL(gamma || p_t) approximately 0.4868, exceeding d/3. These appear locally repairable, but require correction in a theoretical submission.

Significance of the efficiency claims: Proposition 6.1 establishes an O(epsilon^-2 log(1/epsilon)) step bound only for the corrector targeting p_T1. There is no complete discretization bound accounting for reverse-ODE error, early stopping, and estimator-dependent stability constants, so the comparison with end-to-end epsilon^-4 guarantees does not establish an overall computational improvement. Likewise, logarithmic dimension dependence is established for the prescribed forward horizon; the full error bound also contains sqrt(d tau) and exponential stability factors.

Empirical reproducibility and evidence: Figure 1 omits the chosen T1, estimator architecture and training procedure, integration settings, sample counts, Wasserstein estimation method, and meaning of the error bars. The three toy examples provide qualitative illustration, but cannot substantiate the claim that clipping is unnecessary or that the exponential-moment loss is small. An accuracy-versus-computation comparison would also be needed to support practical efficiency claims.
